scenes.headline: How a coding agent keeps its prompt cache warm
scenes.sub: Where eight open harnesses put the cache marker, and why order matters.
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Mullion! Here is how coding agents lay out a request so the provider can skip most of it.

scenes.text: A provider reuses work only for an unchanged prefix, so a harness puts stable blocks first and appends every change after the history.
scenes.say: A provider only reuses work for a prefix it has seen before. So the harness keeps the start of the request still, and appends every change at the end.

steps.say: Every request opens with the same blocks. The tool definitions, the system prompt, and the project memory.
Then the conversation, which only ever grows, and the newest turn at the very end.
A cache marker on the last block tells the provider to save everything up to that point.
On the next request, the whole old prefix comes back as a cheap read. Only the new turn is fresh work.

scenes.title: When something near the top changes

left.title: Edit the head
items: Date written into the system prompt
A new tool rewrites the tool list
left.say: Write the date into the system prompt, or add a tool, and every token after that point has to be processed again.

right.title: Append at the tail
items: Time goes in the latest message
right.say: The newer harnesses append instead. Codex, pi and opencode put updates after the history, so the old prefix still matches.

steps.say: Anthropic bills a request in bands. Tokens up to the highest hit are cache reads. After that come cache writes.
When nothing before the marker changed, the whole prefix is a read.

scenes.title: Input cost of 40 requests on Sonnet 4.6
scenes.say: My cost model for one session on Sonnet four point six. A stable layout costs about fifteen percent of no caching. A timestamp at the top costs more than no caching at all.

scenes.text: Keep the start of the request still for the whole session, and put anything that changes after the history.
